nordamerika.explanation: "Nordamerika" means "North America". It is built from "nord" (north) and "Amerika" (America). To say where you travel to, use "til" (to): "Vi flyver til Nordamerika" (We fly to North America).

norden.explanation: "Norden" means "the Nordic countries". It is the name for Denmark, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Iceland together. It comes from "nord" (north).

nordisk.explanation: "Nordisk" means "Nordic". It comes from "nord" (north). To talk about food from this region, say: "Vi elsker nordisk mad" (We love Nordic food). "Norsk" is a different word and means "Norwegian": "Han er norsk" (He is Norwegian).

nordlig.explanation: "Nordlig" means "northerly". It comes from "nord" (north). To say where in a country a place lies, add "-e" after "det" (the): "Skagen ligger i det nordlige Danmark" (Skagen is in the northern part of Denmark).

nordlys.explanation: "Nordlys" means "northern lights". It takes "et": "et nordlys". It is built from "nord" (north) and "lys" (light). To say you want to see them, say: "Jeg vil gerne se nordlys" (I would like to see the northern lights).

nordpå.explanation: "Nordpå" means "north". It is built from "nord" (north) and "på" (on). To say a train goes in that direction, say: "Toget kører nordpå" (The train goes north). To say where a place is located, use "i nord" (in the north): "Skoven ligger i nord" (The forest lies in the north).

nordsøen.explanation: "Nordsøen" means "the North Sea". It is the sea along the west coast of "Jylland" (Jutland). Danes also call this sea "Vesterhavet" (literally, "the Western Sea").

norge.explanation: "Norge" means "Norway". The language is called "norsk" (Norwegian). To say you speak it, say: "Jeg taler norsk" (I speak Norwegian).

normal.explanation: "Normal" means "normal". To say something is nothing unusual, add "-t" after "det er" (it is): "Det er helt normalt" (That is completely normal).

norsk.explanation: "Norsk" means "Norwegian", for things from Norway. It comes from "Norge" (Norway). When you talk about the language, use it as a name: "Jeg taler norsk" (I speak Norwegian).

nougat.explanation: "Nougat" means "nougat". To ask whether a chocolate has it inside, say: "Er der nougat i chokoladen?" (Is there nougat in the chocolate?)

november.explanation: "November" means "November". To give a date, say the day first: "den første november" (the first of November).

nu.explanation: "Nu" means "now". To say something is happening at this moment, add "lige" (just) before it: "Jeg arbejder lige nu" (I am working right now).

nu skal du høre.explanation: "Nu skal du høre" means "now listen", literally "now you shall hear". To start telling something, say: "Nu skal du høre, hvad der skete i går" (Now listen to what happened yesterday). To speak to several people, change "du" (you) to "I" (you all): "Nu skal I høre!" (Now listen, all of you!)

nudler.explanation: "Nudler" means "noodles". To name a soup made with them, join the words: "en nudelsuppe" (a noodle soup).

nul.explanation: "Nul" means "zero". To give a sports score, it also means "nil": "Vi vinder to–nul" (We win two–nil).

nutid.explanation: "En nutid" means "a present tense". It is built from "nu" (now) and "tid" (time). To show a verb in the present tense, say: "jeg løber" (I run).

nutiden.explanation: "Nutiden" means "the present". It is built from "nu" (now) and "tiden" (the time). To talk about the young people of today, say: "nutidens unge" (the young people of today).

nutildags.explanation: "Nutildags" means "nowadays". To compare today with the past, say: "Nutildags har alle en telefon" (Nowadays everyone has a phone). A spelling with three words also exists, "nu til dags", with the same meaning.

nuttet.explanation: "Nuttet" means "cute". To say how cute something is, start with "hvor" (how): "Hvor er den nuttet!" (How cute it is!)

nuvel.explanation: "Nuvel" means "very well". It is built from "nu" (now) and "vel" (well). To accept something and move on, say: "Nuvel, så gør vi det" (Very well, we will do it that way).

nuværende.explanation: "Nuværende" means "current". It comes from "nu" (now). To talk about who runs a country now, say: "den nuværende regering" (the current government).

ny.explanation: "Ny" means "new". It is also part of "nytår" (New Year). To wish someone a happy New Year, say: "Godt nytår!" (Happy New Year!)

nyheder.explanation: "Nyheder" means "news". For one piece of news, use "en nyhed" (a piece of news): "Jeg har en god nyhed" (I have a piece of good news). To say the news is bad, Danish uses the plural: "Nyhederne er dårlige" (The news is bad).

nylig.explanation: "Nylig" means "recently". It is built from "ny" (new). It is used in the phrase "for nylig", with "for" (for) in front: "Jeg mødte hende for nylig" (I met her recently).

nysgerrig.explanation: "Nysgerrig" means "curious", as in wanting to know things. To say what you are curious to do, add "efter at" (to): "Han er nysgerrig efter at lære mere" (He is curious to learn more). A second meaning is "nosy", as in asking too much about other people: "Vær ikke så nysgerrig!" (Do not be so nosy!)

nysgerrighed.explanation: "En nysgerrighed" means "curiosity". It comes from "nysgerrig" (curious) with "-hed" added, like "-ness" in English. The same ending turns "fri" (free) into "en frihed" (a freedom).

nytte.explanation: "En nytte" means "a use". To say something helps, use "at gøre nytte" (literally, "to do use"): "Paraplyen gjorde nytte" (The umbrella was useful). To say something is of no use, use "ingen" (no): "Det har ingen nytte" (It is of no use).

nyttig.explanation: "Nyttig" means "useful". It comes from "nytte" (use). To say a piece of advice helps, say: "Det er et nyttigt tip" (That is a useful tip).

nytårsaften.explanation: "Nytårsaften" means "New Year's Eve". It is built from "nytår" (new year) and "aften" (evening). On that evening the Danish monarch gives a speech on television, "nytårstalen" (the New Year's speech).

nå.explanation: "Nå" means "oh". When you have just understood something, say: "Nå, det vidste jeg ikke!" (Oh, I did not know that!) To start a chat again, it also means "well": "Nå, hvad så?" (Well, what's up?)

nå ja.explanation: "Nå ja" means "oh right". When you suddenly remember something, say it first: "Nå ja, nu husker jeg det" (Oh right, now I remember). The small word "jo" (as you know) can follow: "Nå ja, det er jo tirsdag i dag" (Oh right, it is Tuesday today, you know).

nå men.explanation: "Nå men" means "well then". To move a conversation on, say: "Nå men, lad os komme i gang" (Well then, let us get started). To end a conversation, say: "Nå men, jeg må videre" (Well then, I have to move on).

nåde.explanation: "En nåde" means "a mercy". To say a person is merciful, use "at vise nåde" (to show mercy): "Dommeren viste nåde" (The judge showed mercy). A second meaning is "grace": "af Guds nåde" (by the grace of God).

når.explanation: "Når" means "when". For something that happens again and again or has not happened yet, use it like this: "Når det regner, bliver jeg hjemme" (When it rains, I stay home). For one time in the past, use "da" (when): "Da jeg kom hjem, var det mørkt" (When I came home, it was dark). To ask a question, use "hvornår" (when): "Hvornår kommer du?" (When are you coming?)

når som helst.explanation: "Når som helst" means "anytime". To invite someone, say: "Kom når som helst" (Come anytime). To say something might happen without warning, it also means "at any moment": "Det kan regne når som helst" (It can rain at any moment).

næppe.explanation: "Næppe" means "unlikely". To say something will probably not happen, put it after the verb: "Han kommer næppe" (He is unlikely to come). It also means "hardly": "Jeg kan næppe kende ham" (I can hardly recognize him). A tiny chance is left, unlike "aldrig" (never): "Han kommer aldrig" (He never comes).

nær.explanation: "Nær" means "close". To talk about a person you are close to, put it before the noun: "en nær ven" (a close friend). To say a place is close to something, use "tæt på" (close to): "Jeg bor tæt på stationen" (I live close to the station).

nærig.explanation: "Nærig" means "stingy". It is not a compliment. Do not mix it up with "sparsommelig", which means "thrifty": "Hun er sparsommelig og køber brugt" (She is thrifty and buys second-hand).

næringsrig.explanation: "Næringsrig" means "nutritious". It is built from "en næring" (nourishment) and "rig" (rich). To say a meal is nutritious, say: "Det er et næringsrigt måltid" (It is a nutritious meal).

nærmest.explanation: "Nærmest" means "almost". To say you have nearly finished, say: "Jeg er nærmest færdig" (I am almost done). A second meaning is "nearest": "den nærmeste station" (the nearest station).

nærværende.explanation: "Nærværende" means "attentive". To say a father gives you his full attention, say: "Han er en nærværende far" (He is an attentive father). In a formal contract, "nærværende kontrakt" means "this contract".

næseblod.explanation: "Næseblod" means "a nosebleed". It is built from "næse" (nose) and "blod" (blood). To say you have a nosebleed, leave out the article: "Jeg har næseblod" (I have a nosebleed).

næsten.explanation: "Næsten" means "almost". To say you have nearly finished, say: "Jeg er næsten færdig" (I am almost done). Do not mix it up with "næste", which means "next": "næste uge" (next week).

næsten aldrig.explanation: "Næsten aldrig" means "almost never". It is built from "næsten" (almost) and "aldrig" (never). Because "aldrig" already makes the sentence negative, do not add "ikke" (not). To say you rarely do something, say: "Hun spiser næsten aldrig kød" (She almost never eats meat).

nødder.explanation: "Nødder" means "nuts". To name one kind of nut, join its name to "nød": "en hasselnød" (a hazelnut) and "en valnød" (a walnut).

nødhjælp.explanation: "Nødhjælp" means "emergency aid". It is built from "nød" (distress) and "hjælp" (help). To say you collect money for victims of a disaster, say: "Vi samler nødhjælp ind til ofrene" (We collect emergency aid for the victims).

nødig.explanation: "Nødig" means "rather not". Put it after "vil" (will, want) or "ville" (would): "Jeg vil nødig tage afsted" (I would rather not leave). To say someone else would rather not, say: "Hun ville nødig sige det" (She would rather not say it).

nødt til.explanation: "Nødt til" means "have to". When you have no choice, say "er nødt til at" before the verb: "Jeg er nødt til at gå" (I have to go). When you choose to go, say "Jeg vil gå" (I want to go) instead.

nødvendig.explanation: "Nødvendig" means "necessary". To say you cannot do without something, say: "Et pas er nødvendigt" (A passport is necessary). Do not mix it up with "vigtig", which means "important": "Sundhed er vigtig" (Health is important).

nødvendigvis.explanation: "Nødvendigvis" means "necessarily". It comes from "nødvendig" (necessary). To say something is not always true, put "ikke" (not) before it: "Han er ikke nødvendigvis rig" (He is not necessarily rich).

nøgen.explanation: "Nøgen" means "naked". For trees, it also means "bare": "nøgne træer" (bare trees).

nøgtern.explanation: "Nøgtern" means "matter-of-fact". A second meaning is "sober", as in plain and without drama: "nøgterne tal" (sober figures). To say someone has not been drinking, use "ædru" (sober): "Han er ædru" (He is sober).

nøjagtig.explanation: "Nøjagtig" means "exact". A second meaning is "accurate", as in correct in every detail: "Vi har brug for nøjagtige oplysninger" (We need accurate information).

nøjagtigt.explanation: "Nøjagtigt" means "exactly". It comes from "nøjagtig" (exact). To say a number is not exact, use "omtrent" (about): "Der kom omtrent tre hundrede mennesker" (About three hundred people came).

nøje.explanation: "Nøje" means "closely". To tell someone to read with full attention, say: "Læs kontrakten nøje" (Read the contract closely). To say something is not important, use it with "ikke så" (not so): "Det er ikke så nøje" (It does not matter that much).

at observere.explanation: "At observere" means "to observe". To say you watch animals in nature, say: "at observere fuglene" (to observe the birds).

at offentliggøre.explanation: "At offentliggøre" means "to publish / make public". It is built from "offentlig" (public) and "at gøre" (to make). To say an official body makes something known, say: "Regeringen offentliggør planen" (The government makes the plan public).

at ofre.explanation: "At ofre" means "to sacrifice". To say you give up something valuable for others, say: "Hun ofrer sin weekend" (She gives up her weekend). To say someone makes an offering to a god, say: "at ofre til guderne" (to make an offering to the gods).

at omdanne.explanation: "At omdanne" means "to transform". To say what something becomes, add "til" (into): "De omdanner fabrikken til boliger" (They transform the factory into homes).

at omfatte.explanation: "At omfatte" means "to include". It is built from "om" (around) and "at fatte" (to grasp). To say what a price covers, say: "Prisen omfatter morgenmad" (The price includes breakfast).

at omformulere.explanation: "At omformulere" means "to rephrase". The "om" at the start works like "re-" in "at omskrive" (to rewrite). When someone did not understand you, ask: "Kan du omformulere det?" (Can you rephrase that?)

at omgive.explanation: "At omgive" means "to surround". To say what a place is surrounded by, use "omgivet af" (surrounded by): "Huset er omgivet af skov" (The house is surrounded by forest).

at omgå.explanation: "At omgå" means "to bypass / get around". To say you get around a difficulty, say: "Vi omgår problemet" (We get around the problem). Do not mix it up with "at omgås", which means "to socialize": "Jeg omgås mine kolleger" (I socialize with my colleagues).

at omgås.explanation: "At omgås" means "to associate with / socialize". To say who you spend time with, say: "Jeg omgås mest folk fra arbejdet" (I mostly spend time with people from work). Do not mix it up with "at omgå", which means "to bypass": "Lastbilen omgår byen" (The truck goes around the town).

at omringe.explanation: "At omringe" means "to surround". It is built from "om" (around) and "ring" (ring). To say a crowd closes in on something, say: "Folk omringede scenen" (People surrounded the stage).

at omstille sig.explanation: "At omstille sig" means "to adapt". It needs "sig" (yourself), which changes with the person: "jeg omstiller mig" (I adapt) and "de omstiller sig" (they adapt). To say what you adapt to, add "til" (to): "Vi må omstille os til nye regler" (We have to adapt to new rules).

at omstrukturere.explanation: "At omstrukturere" means "to restructure". The "om" at the start works like "re-" in "at omskrive" (to rewrite). To say a city changes how its schools are organized, say: "Kommunen omstrukturerer sine skoler" (The city is restructuring its schools).

at omtale.explanation: "At omtale" means "to mention / refer to". To say you mention a topic, say: "Han omtalte aldrig ulykken" (He never mentioned the accident). To say how someone is described, add "som" (as): "Hun omtales som byens bedste kok" (She is referred to as the best cook in town).

at opbevare.explanation: "At opbevare" means "to store". On a food label, the instruction to store something in a cool place reads: "Opbevares køligt" (Store in a cool place).

at opbygge.explanation: "At opbygge" means "to build up". It is built from "op" (up) and "at bygge" (to build). To say you grow trust slowly, say: "Vi opbygger tillid" (We build up trust). For a house, use "at bygge" instead: "Vi bygger et hus" (We are building a house).

at opdage.explanation: "At opdage" means "to discover". To say you notice a thing, say: "Jeg opdagede en fejl" (I noticed a mistake). To say you find out that something happened, add "at" (that): "Hun opdagede, at tasken var væk" (She discovered that the bag was gone).

at opdatere.explanation: "At opdatere" means "to update". To remind someone to keep a program current, say: "Husk at opdatere appen" (Remember to update the app).

at opdele.explanation: "At opdele" means "to divide". To say you split something into parts, add "i" (into): "Læreren opdeler klassen i fire hold" (The teacher splits the class into four teams). Do not mix it up with "at dele", which means "to share": "Jeg deler kagen med dig" (I share the cake with you).

at opdrage.explanation: "At opdrage" means "to raise (a child)". To say who raises the children, say: "Hun opdrager sine børn alene" (She raises her children alone).

at operere.explanation: "At operere" means "to operate", as in surgery. To say a doctor performs surgery, say: "Lægen opererer i morgen" (The doctor operates tomorrow). A second meaning is a business working in a place: "Firmaet opererer i Europa" (The company operates in Europe).

at opfange.explanation: "At opfange" means "to pick up / catch". It is built from "op" (up) and "at fange" (to catch). To say a device does not receive a signal, say: "Radioen opfanger ikke signalet her" (The radio does not pick up the signal here).

at opfatte.explanation: "At opfatte" means "to perceive". To ask how someone sees a person or a situation, say: "Hvordan opfatter du ham?" (How do you see him?) To say you did not catch words you heard, say: "Jeg opfattede ikke navnet" (I did not catch the name).

at opfinde.explanation: "At opfinde" means "to invent". It is built from "op" (up) and "at finde" (to find). A second meaning is "to make up": "Han opfandt en undskyldning" (He made up an excuse).

at opfordre.explanation: "At opfordre" means "to urge / encourage". To say who is urged to do what, add "til at" (to) before the verb: "Politiet opfordrer folk til at blive hjemme" (The police urge people to stay at home). Do not mix it up with "at opmuntre", which means "to cheer up": "Hun opmuntrede mig" (She cheered me up).

at opfylde.explanation: "At opfylde" means "to fulfill". It is built from "op" (up) and "at fylde" (to fill). To say you keep a promise, say: "Han opfylder sit løfte" (He fulfills his promise).

at opføre.explanation: "At opføre" means "to build / perform". To say a building is put up, say: "Kommunen opfører en ny skole" (The council is building a new school). To say a play is put on, say: "Teatret opfører et stykke" (The theater is putting on a play). With "sig" (oneself), it means "to behave": "at opføre sig pænt" (to behave nicely).

at opføre sig.explanation: "At opføre sig" means "to behave". To say how someone behaves, add a word like "pænt" (nicely) or "dårligt" (badly): "Han opfører sig dårligt" (He behaves badly). Without "sig" (oneself), "at opføre" means "to build": "De opfører et hus" (They are building a house).

at opgive.explanation: "At opgive" means "to give up". To say you stop trying, say: "Hun opgav at finde nøglen" (She gave up looking for the key). A second meaning is "to state": "at opgive et navn" (to give a name).

at opgradere.explanation: "At opgradere" means "to upgrade". To say you move to a better plan, say: "Jeg opgraderer mit abonnement" (I upgrade my subscription). For making something better in any way, use "at forbedre" (to improve): "Vi forbedrer servicen" (We improve the service).

at opgøre.explanation: "At opgøre" means "to calculate / settle". It is built from "op" (up) and "at gøre" (to do). To say you work out the final accounts, say: "opgøre regnskabet" (settle the accounts). To say you work out how bad a loss is, say: "opgøre skaden" (calculate the damage).

at ophæve.explanation: "At ophæve" means "to repeal / lift". To say a law is ended officially, say: "ophæve en lov" (repeal a law). To say a rule stops applying, say: "ophæve en regel" (lift a rule).

at ophøre.explanation: "At ophøre" means "to cease". To say something ends at a time, say: "Støjen ophører klokken ti" (The noise ceases at ten). To tell someone to stop, use "at holde op" (to stop): "Hold op!" (Stop it!)

at opklare.explanation: "At opklare" means "to solve (a case)". To say you find out what happened, say: "Vi må opklare, hvad der skete" (We must find out what happened). For puzzles and math problems, use "at løse" (to solve): "Jeg løser opgaven" (I solve the exercise).

at oplade.explanation: "At oplade" means "to charge", as in a battery. To say you charge a device, say: "Jeg oplader min computer" (I charge my computer). The shorter "at lade" (to charge) also exists: "Jeg lader min telefon" (I am charging my phone).

at opleve.explanation: "At opleve" means "to experience". It is built from "op" (up) and "at leve" (to live). To say something happened to you, say: "Vi oplevede en flot solnedgang" (We experienced a beautiful sunset).

at oplyse.explanation: "At oplyse" means "to inform / light up". To say an authority gives facts, say: "Politiet oplyser, at manden er fundet" (The police say the man has been found). To say light shines on a place, say: "Månen oplyser vejen" (The moon lights up the road).

at oplære.explanation: "At oplære" means "to train", as in teaching someone a job. To say a person is shown how to do the work, say: "Butikken oplærer ham i at bruge kassen" (The store trains him to use the register). For sports and exercise, use "at træne" (to work out): "Jeg træner hver dag" (I work out every day).

at opmuntre.explanation: "At opmuntre" means "to encourage / cheer up". To say someone gives a person courage, say: "Læreren opmuntrede hende til at prøve igen" (The teacher encouraged her to try again). Do not mix it up with "at opfordre", which means "to urge": "Politiet opfordrer folk til at blive hjemme" (The police urge people to stay at home).

at opnå.explanation: "At opnå" means "to achieve". To say you reach a result, say: "at opnå et godt resultat" (to achieve a good result). To say people reach an agreement, say: "at opnå enighed" (to come to an agreement).

at opprioritere.explanation: "At opprioritere" means "to prioritize higher". The "op" at the start works like "up" in English. To say elder care gets more attention, say: "opprioritere ældreplejen" (give elder care higher priority).

at opretholde.explanation: "At opretholde" means "to maintain". To say the police keep things calm, say: "Politiet opretholder ordenen" (The police maintain order). To say you keep contact going, say: "Vi må opretholde kontakten" (We must keep up the contact). For a building or machine kept in repair, use "at vedligeholde" (to keep in repair): "Vi vedligeholder maskinen" (We maintain the machine).

at oprette.explanation: "At oprette" means "to set up / create". To say you make an account, say: "Jeg opretter en konto" (I create an account). To put a thing in place, such as a shelf, use "at opsætte" (to put up): "Jeg opsætter hylden" (I put up the shelf).

at opsige.explanation: "At opsige" means "to cancel / terminate". To say you give notice on a home, say: "Jeg har opsagt min lejlighed" (I have given notice on my apartment). To say you resign from your job, say: "Jeg opsiger min stilling" (I resign from my job).

at opstille.explanation: "At opstille" means "to set up / nominate". To say things are put in position, say: "Vi opstiller teltet" (We set up the tent). To say a party puts someone forward for election, say: "Partiet opstiller Lars til valget" (The party puts Lars forward for the election).
